item.title: Tyre Nichols
item.description: Last night, police in Memphis released footage of officers beating Tyre Nichols, a 29-year-old Black man, after stopping him in his car earlier this month. He died in hospital three days later. The five officers involved have been sacked and charged with second-degree murder, and people who’ve watched the footage describe it as horrifying. Tyre’s family asked people to protest peacefully, and despite the anger, the protests across the US have largely stayed that way, which says a lot about the strength of his mother and stepfather. I haven’t watched the footage and don’t think I will, but I’m thinking of his family, who should never have had to see their son’s final moments become national news.

item.title: Ordinary People
item.description: Today is Holocaust Memorial Day, 78 years since Auschwitz-Birkenau was liberated, and this year’s theme is “Ordinary People.” It’s about how the Holocaust wasn’t carried out by monsters alone, but made possible by ordinary people who took part, looked away or stayed quiet, and also how ordinary people sometimes risked everything to help. Six million Jewish people were murdered, along with Roma and Sinti, disabled people, gay men and many others, and the number of survivors still able to tell their stories gets smaller every year. After seeing a huge celebrity post a swastika to millions of people only a few weeks ago, it feels more important than ever to remember, and to call out antisemitism and hatred wherever it shows up. Tonight I’m thinking of the people who were lost, and promising myself not to be one of those who look away.

item.title: The Morning After
item.description: The morning after Germany and the US promised tanks to Ukraine, Russia launched another big wave of missiles and drones across the country, killing several people and hitting power supplies again. Ukraine’s air defences shot down most of them, which shows why the air defence systems allies have sent matter so much, but each strike that gets through still costs lives. It feels like every bit of help from Ukraine’s allies is met with more attacks on ordinary people and the things they need to get through winter. Tomorrow is Holocaust Memorial Day, a reminder of what happens when the world looks away from cruelty. Tonight I’m thinking of everyone in Ukraine who is cold and in the dark, hoping the help arrives soon.

item.title: Leopards
item.description: Reports tonight say Germany has finally decided to send Leopard 2 tanks to Ukraine, and to let other countries like Poland send theirs too, after weeks of debate and pressure from allies. There are also reports that the US will send its own Abrams tanks, which seems to be what Germany wanted before it would move. Ukraine has been asking for modern tanks for months, and they could make a big difference to its chances of pushing Russian forces back in the spring. It’s been a long, frustrating wait, especially after the UK committed Challenger 2s ten days ago, but if the reports are right, this is a real turning point in Western support. After a heavy few weeks of news from Ukraine, tonight feels a bit more hopeful.

item.title: Ethics Adviser
item.description: Sunak has asked his independent ethics adviser to investigate whether Conservative Party chairman Nadhim Zahawi broke the ministerial code over his tax affairs. Zahawi has confirmed he settled with HMRC, reportedly for millions of pounds including a penalty, while he was Chancellor last summer, and he says he’ll cooperate fully. His supporters say he has paid what he owed and should be allowed to carry on, while critics say someone in charge of the country’s finances shouldn’t have been in a dispute with the tax authorities at all. Sunak came in promising “integrity, professionalism and accountability,” so how this turns out will be a real test of that. For now, Zahawi stays in his job while the investigation takes place.

item.title: Monterey Park
item.description: Last night, as Lunar New Year celebrations were finishing in Monterey Park, a largely Asian American city near Los Angeles, a gunman opened fire at a dance studio and killed ten people. The man suspected of the attack was later found dead in a van, and people are still trying to understand why it happened. On a day that should have been about family, fireworks and new beginnings, an entire community is grieving instead. It’s horribly familiar to see another mass shooting in the US, and I don’t think anyone should ever get used to it, however often it happens. Tonight I’m thinking of the families in Monterey Park, and I hope the Year of the Rabbit brings them some peace.

item.title: Year of the Rabbit
item.description: Tonight is Lunar New Year’s Eve, and tomorrow the Year of the Rabbit begins, which is supposed to be a year of calm, gentleness and hope. In China, it’s the first new year in three years without Covid restrictions, so hundreds of millions of people are travelling home to see family, many for the first time since the pandemic began. After everything that happened there in the autumn, from lockdown protests to blank sheets of paper, I really hope these reunions are as joyful as they deserve to be. Communities here are celebrating too, with lanterns, dumplings and dragon dances getting ready across the country. After the year we’ve had, a gentle Year of the Rabbit sounds pretty perfect to me, so happy Lunar New Year to everyone celebrating.

item.title: Buckle Up
item.description: Rishi Sunak has been fined by Lancashire Police for not wearing a seatbelt while filming a social media video in the back of a moving car, his second police fine after Partygate. He’s apologised and called it a brief error of judgement, which is fair enough, but it’s hard to believe nobody in that car thought to mention it while the camera was rolling. In tech, Google’s parent company announced it’s cutting 12,000 jobs, two days after Microsoft’s 10,000, so this is turning into a really grim month for people in the industry. At a big meeting of Ukraine’s allies in Germany, there was still no agreement on sending German-made Leopard tanks, even after the UK committed Challenger 2s last weekend, which must be frustrating for Ukraine given everything this week has shown. So it’s a Friday that ends with a reminder to buckle up, back up your CV, and hope the tanks arrive soon.

item.title: Brovary
item.description: This morning a helicopter crashed next to a kindergarten in Brovary, just outside Kyiv, killing Ukraine’s Interior Minister Denys Monastyrskyi, other senior officials and people on the ground, including children. Nobody yet knows why it came down, and Ukraine says it’s investigating, but the thought of it falling at a nursery while children were arriving for the day is almost too much. It comes only four days after the missile strike on the apartment block in Dnipro, so it’s been a brutal week for Ukraine. Here, nurses were on strike today and are out again tomorrow, which is a real problem, but tonight it feels small compared to what people there are going through. I’m thinking of the families in Brovary.

item.title: Ruthless
item.description: After yesterday’s David Carrick case, the Metropolitan Police has said it’s reviewing 1,633 past allegations of sexual offences or domestic abuse involving 1,071 of its own officers and staff, cases that didn’t lead to prosecution or dismissal. Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley says the force “failed,” that hundreds of officers are likely to lose their jobs, and that every one of the Met’s 45,000 officers and staff will be checked again against police records. Carrick himself was formally sacked today, which feels like the absolute least that should have happened years ago. It’s right that they’re finally looking, but it’s frightening that it took a case this horrific to make it happen, and that so many of those people are still in their jobs while the review goes on. For anyone who’s been let down by the police, and especially women who weren’t believed, I hope this is the start of real change rather than another apology.

item.title: He Should Never Have Been an Officer
item.description:
Content note: this post mentions sexual violence.

Today a serving Metropolitan Police officer, David Carrick, admitted 49 offences against 12 women over nearly two decades, including 24 counts of rape, using his job to make them afraid that nobody would believe them. The Met has admitted he came to the attention of police nine times before he was finally arrested in 2021, including allegations of rape and domestic abuse, and nothing was done, and it has publicly apologised. He served in the same armed unit as Sarah Everard’s murderer, which makes it even harder to take. The women who came forward did something incredibly brave, and it’s heartbreaking that the people meant to protect them failed so badly for so long. Real change has to start with listening to women the first time, and if this case has brought up anything difficult for you, organisations like Rape Crisis are there to help.

item.title: Two Places
item.description: A passenger plane carrying 72 people crashed this morning as it came in to land at Pokhara in Nepal, and it’s feared nobody survived, making it Nepal’s deadliest air crash in decades. Video shared online shows it banking sharply just before it went down, and it’s unbearable to think about the families waiting for news. In Dnipro, rescuers have spent a second day digging through the ruins of the apartment block hit by a Russian missile yesterday, and the number of people killed keeps rising, though they’ve also pulled some survivors from the rubble. It’s a hard day to be reading the news, and I almost didn’t want to write about it at all. But I think remembering the people who’ve been lost matters, so tonight I’m thinking of Pokhara and Dnipro.

item.title: Dnipro
item.description: Today the UK confirmed it will send Challenger 2 tanks to Ukraine, the first Western country to promise modern battle tanks, after Sunak spoke to Zelensky. Hours later, a Russian missile hit a nine-storey apartment block in Dnipro, collapsing part of it and killing many people, with rescuers still searching through the rubble for survivors tonight. The pictures of a building torn open, with people’s kitchens and bedrooms just hanging there, are going to stay with me for a long time. These were families at home on a Saturday afternoon, not soldiers, and it’s exactly why Ukraine keeps asking for better air defences and support. Tonight my heart is with Dnipro.

item.title: Friday the 13th
item.description: It’s Friday the 13th, which seems appropriate for a week in which Royal Mail has been hit by a cyber attack that has stopped it sending letters and parcels abroad. It’s reportedly the work of the LockBit ransomware gang, who encrypt a company’s systems and then demand money to unlock them, and it’s left small businesses that rely on overseas orders stuck with piles of packages they can’t send. It’s frightening how much damage one attack can do to an organisation that’s been around for more than 500 years, especially at a time when it’s already struggling with strikes. If there’s a lesson for the rest of us, it’s that the boring stuff really matters: keeping things updated, having offline backups, using proper passwords and multi-factor authentication, and training people to spot dodgy emails. Away from all the screens, fighting in eastern Ukraine around a town called Soledar has been some of the fiercest of the war, so I’m keeping things in perspective tonight.

item.title: One Damaged File
item.description: This afternoon our time, every domestic flight in the US was grounded for a while after a system that sends safety notices to pilots stopped working, the first nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Thousands of flights were delayed or cancelled, and early reports suggest the cause was a single damaged database file. As someone who works around IT systems, that’s the kind of thing that makes me wince, because it shows how much depends on old, important systems that people don’t think about until they break. It’s a good reminder to test your backups, avoid single points of failure, and never assume that because something has always worked, it always will. Back home, ambulance workers were on strike again today, so it’s been a tough day for the people keeping things running in every sense.

item.title: So Close
item.description: Last night was supposed to be a historic moment for the UK, the first ever attempt to launch satellites into orbit from British soil. Virgin Orbit’s modified 747, called Cosmic Girl, took off from Spaceport Cornwall in Newquay and released its rocket over the Atlantic, but something went wrong with the rocket’s second stage and the nine satellites it was carrying were lost. The crowd who’d gone to watch in the cold had been so excited, and you could hear the disappointment in the coverage this morning. It’s a real shame for everyone who worked on it, especially as it was meant to show the UK could have its own space launch industry. Space is hard, though, and almost every big launch programme has failures early on, so I hope they get to try again.

item.title: The Morning After
item.description: The day after the attack on Brazil’s government buildings, around 1,500 people have been detained, and Lula has walked through the wrecked rooms of the presidential palace with officials. Brazil’s Supreme Court has suspended the governor of the capital’s region for 90 days, after questions about why security let the crowds get so close. Bolsonaro himself is in hospital in Florida with stomach pains, and has said on social media that the riots went beyond peaceful protest, though critics say he spent years encouraging the idea that the election would be stolen. Leaders around the world, from left and right, have condemned the attack and backed Lula, which is reassuring. After two days of watching it all, I’m grateful our own fights about strikes and pay are happening through talks and picket lines rather than broken windows.

item.title: Brasília
item.description: Tonight, thousands of Bolsonaro supporters stormed Brazil’s Congress, Supreme Court and presidential palace in Brasília, smashing windows, wrecking offices and refusing to accept that Lula won the election. Two days after the second anniversary of the attack on the US Capitol, the pictures look horribly familiar. Police have taken back the buildings and arrested hundreds of people, and Lula, who was away from the capital, has put the federal government in charge of security there. Watching it, I keep thinking about how fragile democracy is when people are told over and over that an election they lost was stolen. I hope the people responsible are held to account and that Brazil can calm down from here.

item.title: Coming Home
item.description: From midnight in China, which was this afternoon our time, people arriving from abroad no longer have to quarantine, ending almost three years of some of the strictest border rules in the world. For millions of families who haven’t been able to see each other since the start of the pandemic, that must be an enormous relief, especially with the Lunar New Year coming up in a few weeks. It comes while cases in China are reportedly surging, though, and several countries, including the UK, have brought in testing for travellers arriving from there. It’s hard to believe that only six weeks ago people were holding up blank sheets of paper in protest at all this, and now it’s being dropped almost overnight. I hope the reunions are joyful and the hospitals cope.

item.title: Two Years On
item.description: It’s two years today since the attack on the US Capitol, and Biden marked it by giving medals to police officers and election workers who stood up for democracy that day. On the same day, the House of Representatives is still trying to choose a Speaker, now well over a dozen votes in, with Kevin McCarthy winning over most of the Republicans who’d blocked him after agreeing to a lot of their demands. It looks like he might finally get there tonight, though at the cost of giving his critics a lot of power over him. There’s something a bit poetic about the building where that riot happened spending the anniversary proving how messy, slow and frustrating normal democracy is, but that’s still far better than the alternative. I’ll check in the morning to see if they’ve managed it.

item.title: Five Promises
item.description: Sunak gave his first big speech of the year today and set out five promises he wants to be judged on: halve inflation, grow the economy, get debt falling, cut NHS waiting lists, and pass laws to stop small boats crossing the Channel. Supporters say it’s a sensible, measurable plan after the chaos of last autumn, while critics point out that inflation was already expected to fall and that there was nothing new on the nurses’ and ambulance strikes. I like that they’re specific enough that we’ll actually be able to check by the end of the year, which is more than most political speeches manage. Over in the US, the House voted three more times today and still couldn’t pick a Speaker, so that’s six failed rounds now. Between the two, I’m learning a lot more about how other people’s governments work than I ever expected to.

item.title: No Speaker
item.description: Over in Washington, the new US House of Representatives tried to elect a Speaker today and failed three times in a row, the first time in a hundred years that’s taken more than one vote. Republicans won the House in November, but about twenty of their own members refused to back their leader, Kevin McCarthy, so no one reached the 218 votes needed. Until someone is chosen, the House can’t swear in its members or do any business at all, so they’ll keep voting tomorrow. After the autumn we had here, it’s oddly comforting to see that other countries’ politics can get stuck too. Hopefully they sort it out without needing a lettuce.

item.description: It’s the last bank holiday of the festive break, so I’ve spent it doing absolutely nothing and finishing the last of the chocolate. The news is already reminding me that 2023 isn’t starting gently, though: A&E departments are under so much pressure that emergency doctors are warning long delays could be linked to hundreds of extra deaths a week. On top of that, the rail strikes start again tomorrow, just as everyone heads back to work, so a lot of people’s first commute of the year will be a mess. None of last year’s problems disappeared at midnight on Saturday, and the cost of living, the strikes and the NHS are all still here, waiting for us. Still, I’m trying to hold onto a bit of the calm from the last few days, and tomorrow is a new week.

item.title: Hello, 2023
item.description: Happy New Year! The first day of 2023 has been quiet and cosy here, but the world has kept moving: Croatia switched to the euro overnight and joined the Schengen area, so people there woke up with new money in their pockets. In Brazil, Lula was sworn in as president for a third time, and Bolsonaro didn’t even stay to hand over the sash, having flown to Florida instead. After a year that felt like one long shock after another, I’m trying to start this one gently, with fewer late-night news binges and more time with the people I love. My one real resolution is to keep writing here and to keep more of my own stuff on platforms I control, because last year showed how quickly something you rely on can change under you. Here’s to 2023, and to a few more boring days, hopefully.

item.title: Goodbye, 2022
item.description: Even on New Year’s Eve, Russia fired missiles at Kyiv, so Ukrainians are seeing in 2023 with air raid sirens instead of fireworks, and they’re the first people I’m thinking about tonight. Here, London’s fireworks are about to start, including a tribute to the Queen, and it’s going to feel very strange seeing in a new year without her. I’ve written something here almost every day since August, and looking back, it’s turned into a diary of one of the wildest stretches of news I can remember, from lettuces and blue ticks to blank paper and a World Cup final. Thank you to anyone who’s read along, whether you’ve been here since “Hello” or just found me tonight. Happy New Year, I hope 2023 is gentler, kinder and a lot more boring, in the best possible way.

item.title: Looking Back
item.description: Brazil has declared three days of mourning for Pelé, and the New Year Honours came out tonight with the Lionesses rightly all over the list after winning the Euros in the summer. That feels like a good moment to look back on a year that just would not sit still: war returned to Europe, the Queen died, we went through three Prime Ministers and a lettuce, inflation passed 11%, half the country seemed to be on strike, and a billionaire bought the place where we all argued about it. There were bright spots too: Kherson, Morocco’s run, Messi finally getting his World Cup, Hamza on Strictly, and a lot of ordinary people being brave and kind when they didn’t have to be. I started this blog in August as a little daily diary, and somewhere along the way it became my record of a very strange autumn, which I’m glad I kept. One more day of 2022, and I’m hoping 2023 is a bit kinder to all of us.

item.title: Someone Foolish Enough
item.description: Argentina’s World Cup winners got home today to millions of people on the streets of Buenos Aires, so many that the open-top bus couldn’t get through, and the players had to be taken out by helicopter. Seeing the whole country come out for Messi and his teammates was one of the happiest things I’ve seen all year. Meanwhile, Musk has finally responded to his own poll, saying he’ll resign as Twitter’s boss “as soon as I find someone foolish enough to take the job” and that he’ll keep running the software and servers. That’s a very Musk way of keeping his word while hanging on to most of the control. Still, today had a lot of joy in it, and with Christmas getting closer I’m happy to focus on that.

item.title: Not a Choice They Wanted
item.description: Nurses in England, Wales and Northern Ireland walk out again tomorrow, and ambulance workers strike on Wednesday, so this is a really hard week for the NHS just before Christmas. Nobody becomes a nurse or a paramedic because they want to stand on a picket line in the freezing cold, and that so many of them feel they have no other option says a lot. The government says it can’t afford what they’re asking for, and the unions say low pay is driving people out and making care worse for everyone, so it feels completely stuck. Whatever side people are on, I hope everyone who needs care this week gets it, and that there’s a deal soon. If I need anything, I’ll be very nice to whoever looks after me.

item.title: The Greatest Final
item.description: I think I just watched the greatest World Cup final ever. Argentina were 2–0 up and cruising through Messi and Di María, then Mbappé scored twice in two minutes to level it, Messi put Argentina ahead again in extra time, and Mbappé completed the first hat-trick in a men’s World Cup final since 1966. Emiliano Martínez made a ridiculous save in the very last minute, then saved again in the shootout before Gonzalo Montiel scored the winning penalty. Watching Messi finally lift the trophy, after so many years and so much heartbreak, was genuinely emotional, and I don’t even support Argentina. Mbappé deserved so much more than to lose, but tonight belongs to Messi, and after a World Cup with so many difficult questions off the pitch, the football gave us one perfect afternoon.

item.title: Hamza Wins
item.description: Hamza Yassin and Jowita Przystał won the Strictly Come Dancing final tonight, and I don’t think I’ve cheered at the telly that much in ages. Hamza is a wildlife cameraman and CBeebies presenter who’d never really danced before, and over the series he went from nervous to absolutely flying, especially in that salsa. It was just pure, simple joy to watch, and after a month of strikes, fires, lockdown protests, freezing lakes and Twitter meltdowns, it was exactly what I needed. Sometimes the nicest thing you can do is curl up on the sofa with a cup of tea and watch someone you’ve been rooting for get their happy ending. Tomorrow it’s the World Cup final, so the weekend isn’t done yet.

item.title: Red Lines
item.description: Overnight Twitter suspended several journalists from the New York Times, CNN, the Washington Post and others, all of whom had been reporting on the @ElonJet account being banned, with Musk claiming they’d shared “assassination coordinates” by linking to it. It also suspended Mastodon’s own account and started marking links to Mastodon as potentially harmful, which feels like someone trying to stop people finding the exit. The EU’s Věra Jourová has warned of “red lines” and possible sanctions under new EU rules, and the UN has criticised it too. Six weeks ago this platform was supposed to become a free speech haven, and tonight it’s banning reporters and blocking a competitor. If I needed a reason to finally move my main presence somewhere I actually have some control over, this is it.

item.title: Morocco, Thank You
item.description: France beat Morocco 2–0 tonight to reach their second World Cup final in a row, with Theo Hernández scoring in the fifth minute and Randal Kolo Muani adding a second near the end. Morocco never stopped pushing, and even in defeat they made history as the first African and first Arab team to reach a World Cup semi-final. Their run has meant so much to so many people, in Morocco, across Africa and the Arab world, and in Moroccan communities everywhere, and their fans have been the soul of this tournament. They beat Belgium, Spain and Portugal and only lost to the reigning champions, which is an amazing achievement. Morocco have my respect, and I hope they’re welcomed home as heroes.

item.title: One More Game
item.description: Argentina beat Croatia 3–0 tonight to reach the World Cup final, and Messi was magical. He scored a penalty that made him Argentina’s all-time top World Cup scorer, then set up Julián Álvarez’s second goal by spinning one of the best defenders in the tournament around and around before squaring it. Croatia had been so tough to beat all tournament, but tonight they couldn’t get close. It’s very likely Messi’s last World Cup, and after losing the 2014 final, he gets one more chance on Sunday at the only trophy he hasn’t won. I’m not Argentinian, but I’ll be cheering for him.

item.title: Three Boys
item.description: Police confirmed today that three of the boys pulled from the lake in Solihull yesterday have died, aged eight, ten and eleven, and a fourth boy, who is six, is still critically ill in hospital. From what’s been reported, they were friends playing together after school, and some may have gone onto the ice to help each other when it cracked. People have been laying flowers at the park all day, and the police have praised the officer who tried to punch through the ice to reach them and the members of the public who went into the freezing water. There aren’t really words for something like this, and I’ve been holding my own people a little tighter tonight. Please keep talking to children about how dangerous frozen lakes and ponds are, because no family should ever have to go through this.

item.title: Thin Ice
item.description: This afternoon four children were pulled from a frozen lake at Babbs Mill Park in Solihull after falling through the ice, and tonight they’re all in a critical condition in hospital. Emergency crews are still searching the lake in the dark and freezing cold because there are fears more children may have been on the ice. People who were there say members of the public and a police officer went into the water to try to reach them, which is incredibly brave. I keep thinking about the families, who must be living every parent’s worst fear right now, and about how quickly a fun afternoon in the snow turned into this. If you have children in your life, please remind them to keep off frozen water, however solid it looks.

item.title: So Close
item.description: England are out, losing 2–1 to France in the quarter-final, and it really hurts because we were good tonight. Kane scored a penalty to equalise and match Rooney’s record of 53 England goals, but after Giroud put France back ahead, Kane got a second penalty and blasted it over the bar with minutes to go. I can’t imagine how he feels, and I hope people go easy on him, because he’s carried this team for years. The young players like Bellingham, Saka and Foden gave me a lot of hope for the next tournament, so it doesn’t feel like the end of something, more like it’s nearly there. For now I’m putting the kettle on and pretending I’m not gutted.

item.title: Chaos, Then Sadness
item.description: Argentina against the Netherlands was the wildest game of the tournament so far. Argentina were 2–0 up and cruising, then Wout Weghorst came off the bench and scored twice, the second from a clever free-kick routine with almost the last kick of stoppage time, to send it to extra time. It was bad-tempered from start to finish, with a record number of yellow cards and players squaring up even after the shootout, before Lautaro Martínez scored the winning penalty to send Argentina into the semis against Croatia. Then came news that took all the fun out of it: US football journalist Grant Wahl collapsed in the press box during the game and has died. He’d spent years covering the workers who built these stadiums, and he wore a rainbow shirt to a match earlier in the tournament, so tonight I’m thinking of his family more than the football.

item.title: Atlas Lions
item.description: Morocco knocked out Spain on penalties tonight after a 0–0 draw, with goalkeeper Yassine Bounou saving twice and Achraf Hakimi finishing it with a cheeky chipped penalty. That puts Morocco in the quarter-finals for the first time ever, only the fourth African team to get that far, and the celebrations from their fans, across the Arab world and in Morocco’s diaspora everywhere, have been wonderful to watch. Spain had loads of the ball and barely threatened, which feels like their whole tournament in one game. Later, Portugal beat Switzerland 6–1, with Gonçalo Ramos scoring a hat-trick in his first World Cup start, playing in Ronaldo’s place after Ronaldo was dropped to the bench. Morocco against Portugal in the quarters is now one of the games I’m most excited about.

item.title: Dance, Brazil
item.description: Brazil beat South Korea 4–1 tonight, scoring four goals in the first 36 minutes, with Neymar back from injury and every goal followed by a different dance, including the manager Tite joining in. Some people find all the dancing disrespectful, but I loved it, because football is supposed to be fun and they were clearly having the time of their lives. The nicest moment was at the end, when the players held up a banner wishing Pelé well, since he’s in hospital back in Brazil. South Korea deserve credit too for getting out of their group with that late winner against Portugal, even if tonight was too much for them. Brazil play Croatia next, and on this form they look like the team to beat.

The day started on a worrying note, though, with news that Raheem Sterling had flown home to be with his family after an incident at his house. That sets up England against France in the quarter-final on Saturday, which is huge, and I’m already nervous about it.

item.title: One Thousand
item.description: Tonight Lionel Messi played the 1,000th professional match of his career and scored in it, his first ever goal in a World Cup knockout match, as Argentina beat Australia 2–1. It’s wild that someone as good as Messi had never scored in a World Cup knockout game before, and you could see how much it meant to him and to the fans. Australia made it tense at the end, though: a deflected shot made it 2–1, and Emiliano Martínez had to make a huge save in the last minute to stop it going to extra time. Two weeks ago Argentina lost to Saudi Arabia and looked finished, and now they’re in the quarter-finals, which is what makes tournament football so special. England play Senegal tomorrow night, so I’m hoping for something nearly as good.

item.title: Group Stage Goodbye
item.description: The last day of the group stage was absolute chaos. Cameroon beat Brazil 1–0 with an injury-time header from Vincent Aboubakar, who then got sent off for taking his shirt off to celebrate, which might be the most joyful red card I’ve ever seen. South Korea scored a late winner against Portugal to go through, which knocked out Uruguay even though they beat Ghana 2–0, because South Korea had scored more goals, and the Uruguay players ended up surrounding the referee at the end. Brazil and Portugal still went through, so the big names survived, but the smaller teams made them sweat. The knockouts start tomorrow, and England play Senegal on Sunday, so at least I’ll have one good thing to look forward to this weekend.

item.title: There Has to Be a Line
item.description: Kanye West (Ye) has been suspended from Twitter after posting an image of a swastika merged with the Star of David, hours after praising Hitler in a live interview. Musk said he’d “tried his best” but Ye broke the rule against incitement to violence, so the account is gone. There isn’t any room for ambiguity here: antisemitism is hateful and dangerous, and posting a swastika to millions of followers isn’t edgy or free speech, it’s a threat to real people. What strikes me is that a month after promising that Twitter would be a free speech haven and that moderation would go to a council, the call ended up being made personally by one man at midnight. That’s exactly why it matters who runs our platforms, and why I’d rather moderation came from clear, published rules than one person’s mood.

item.title: Hello, ChatGPT
item.description: Post number 600, and tonight my timeline is full of screenshots of something called ChatGPT, a free chatbot OpenAI released today as a “research preview.” People are getting it to write poems, explain code, draft emails and answer questions in a way that sounds surprisingly like a real person, which is a big leap from the clunky chatbots I’m used to. It also gets things confidently wrong, and as someone who cares about who holds our data, I’m wary of typing anything personal into a box run by one company. item.title: The Golden Era Is Over
item.description: Sunak gave his first big foreign policy speech tonight at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet and said the “golden era” of UK–China relations is over, along with the naive idea that trade would lead to social and political reform. Coming after a weekend of people in Shanghai holding up blank paper and a BBC journalist being beaten, the timing could hardly be more pointed. He described China as a “systemic challenge” rather than a threat, and some in his own party are already saying that’s too soft. It’s one of the reasons I like running my own stuff where I can, because it’s a small way of not handing everything to a few companies or governments.

item.description: Tonight the BBC says one of its journalists, Ed Lawrence, was arrested, handcuffed, and beaten and kicked by police while covering the protests in Shanghai, before being released after several hours. There’s footage of him being dragged away and shouting for someone to “call the consulate now,” and the BBC has rejected China’s explanation as not credible. item.title: Urumqi Road
item.description: Tonight videos have been coming out of China showing people protesting against the zero-Covid lockdowns, which is something I never expected to see. It started after a flat fire in Urumqi on Thursday killed ten people, with many asking whether lockdown measures stopped them getting out, and the vigils for the victims turned into protests. In Shanghai, on a street named after Urumqi, crowds have been chanting for the Communist Party and Xi Jinping to step down, a huge risk to take in China. After watching Iran’s players stand silent during their anthem on Monday, it feels like there’s a lot of quiet bravery around at the moment from people who have so much more to lose than I ever will. It’s also a reminder of why open platforms matter, because without people sharing these videos, most of us would never know any of this happened.

item.title: Black Friday, Blue Week
item.description: The Royal College of Nursing announced today that nurses in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will strike on 15 and 20 December, the first time in the union’s 106-year history. When nurses feel they have no choice but to walk out, that tells you how bad things have got. It’s also Black Friday with Royal Mail on strike again, so there’s plenty of shopping but not many deliveries. The football didn’t cheer me up much either: Wales lost 2–0 to Iran after Wayne Hennessey got the first red card of the tournament and Iran scored twice deep into injury time, and England could only draw 0–0 with the USA, so we’ve still never beaten them at a World Cup. Qatar also became the first team knocked out, as hosts, which is quite something. I’m ending the week tired, a bit flat, and thinking about all the nurses who’ll be on a picket line two weeks before Christmas.

item.title: Nobody Saw That Coming
item.description: Saudi Arabia beat Argentina 2–1 today, and it’s already being called one of the biggest shocks in World Cup history. Messi scored an early penalty and it looked like it would be easy, then Saleh Al-Shehri and Salem Al-Dawsari scored within five minutes of each other after half-time, ending Argentina’s 36-game unbeaten run. The Saudi players went wild, the fans went wild, and King Salman has declared tomorrow a public holiday, which is the most extra (and honestly brilliant) reaction to a football match I can imagine. Later, France went a goal down to Australia before winning 4–1, with Olivier Giroud scoring twice to equal Thierry Henry’s record of 51 goals for France. After a weekend that was mostly about armbands and politics, it was really nice to have a day where the football itself was the story.

item.title: Kick-Off
item.description: The World Cup is finally underway, and Qatar became the first host nation ever to lose their opening match, 2–0 to Ecuador, with Enner Valencia scoring both. The BBC didn’t show the opening ceremony on BBC One and opened its coverage with Gary Lineker talking about the human rights concerns instead, which I thought was the right call. It’s been hard to enjoy, though, because I woke up to news of a shooting at Club Q, an LGBTQ+ nightclub in Colorado Springs, where five people were killed the night before Trans Day of Remembrance. England play Iran tomorrow, and I’ll watch, but tonight I’m thinking about the people at Club Q and everyone who just wants to be themselves and stay safe.

item.description: The World Cup starts tomorrow, and for the first time I honestly don’t know how I feel about watching. I love the shared buzz of a tournament, with everyone getting behind England, but there are migrant workers who died building these stadiums, and LGBTQ+ fans being told to be “respectful” in a country where who they are is illegal. Today showed the whole range: a Prime Minister in a snowy warzone promising air defences, a man dying after being held in a centre we’ve known was overcrowded for weeks, climate talks running late, and a billionaire deciding whether to unban a former president with a Twitter poll. I think I’ll watch, but I’ll keep paying attention to the people who don’t get a camera on them. Tonight I’m just grateful for a warm house, the people I love, and the fact that tomorrow is Sunday.

item.title: Przewodów
item.description: This afternoon a missile landed in Przewodów, a small Polish village a few miles from the Ukrainian border, and killed two men at a grain dryer. Poland’s foreign ministry now says it was Russian-made, but nobody yet seems sure who fired it or why, and there’s a lot of speculation that could easily get ahead of the facts. Poland is a NATO country, so the whole evening has been emergency meetings and words like “Article 4” that I only half understood until tonight. What stays with me most is that two ordinary people died doing farm work, on a day when the rest of the news was about summits and population milestones. I’m going to bed hoping the morning brings calm heads and clear answers rather than a rush to escalate.

item.title: Kherson
item.description: Ukrainian troops entered Kherson today after Russia withdrew, and the videos of people in the streets hugging soldiers, waving flags and crying have been on my screen all evening. Kherson was the only regional capital Russia captured after the full invasion began in February, so getting it back is a big deal, and some people are hoping it could be a turning point. It feels fitting that it happened on Armistice Day, the day we remember what war costs and why freedom matters. There’s still a long winter ahead, and Russia has spent the last month bombing power and water, so I don’t want to pretend it’s over. Tonight, though, after a week of shrinking economies, collapsing crypto and Twitter chaos, I’m just going to be glad for the people of Kherson.

item.title: Goodbye, October
item.description: It’s Halloween, and honestly nothing anyone has dressed up as tonight is scarier than the actual news this month. In October we had a Chancellor sacked, a budget torn up, two Home Secretaries (one of them twice), a Prime Minister outlasted by a lettuce, another sworn in without a vote, and a billionaire buy one of the main places we all talk to each other. item.content:
Nearly a month in to the twenty-second season of Fortnite, aka Paradise and I must say I miss Vibin or maybe I just want the summer to come back.

PARADISE. Bold choice of name, that, for a season whose entire plot is a sentient silver liquid steadily eating the island one landmark at a time. If this is paradise then I’d like a word with whoever signed off the brochure, because the brochure said nothing whatsoever about the creeping chrome.

I would like to note, for the record, that I am enjoying myself enormously. I am aware that I announced exactly that in public a week ago, in writing, in a post where I claimed not to have thought about Vibin since the Tuesday. I would like that post struck from the record.

Things I have formed opinions about since:

The season villain is called the Herald, which is a very confident name for somebody who unlocks three quarters of the way through the battle pass. Heralds traditionally arrive before the thing, its literally in the job description.

The new ‘chrome’ guns get better the more damage you do with them, climbing all the way up from Uncommon to Mythic, which is a beautiful system designed with great care for players who hit what they are aiming at. Mine has been Uncommon since the twentieth of September.

There is a block of flats in the sky called Cloudy Condos. Fastest planning approval in recorded history and nobody has said a word about it.

And there’s an item called the Port-A-Bunker, where you throw a bunker on the floor and climb inside it, which is comfortably the most relatable thing they have ever shipped, and I use it constantly, and not always because anybody is shooting at me.

The chrome blob business where you go very fast and stop being hurt by falling off things remains my only real tactic. It is still just running away, only now with sparkles.

If I’m honest with myself, the thing I’m actually missing is August. Vibin was long light evenings and the window open and that daft tree, and Paradise is dark by seven with the heating on and me reading about kilowatt hours for recreation. None of which is the game’s fault, the game is fine, but its just where I happen to notice.

And yes, in a couple of months this one will end as well and I will write a mournful little post about how much I miss the chrome, and I have stopped trying to fight that. Apparently I’m a person who gets sentimental about things that were advertised as temporary from the outset, which is going to serve me beautifully for the rest of my life.

Still terrible at it, but I’m still playing.

item.title: Bone dust
item.description:
The Nobel for medicine went this morning to Svante Pääbo, who worked out how to read the DNA of people who died forty thousand years ago, and I have thought about very little else since about eight.

Here’s the bit that got me, because it isn’t the bit you’d expect.

You’d assume the hard part is that the DNA is old and broken, and it is, it’s in tiny fragments with no instructions attached. But the properly horrible problem is contamination. Bone that old is absolutely full of bacteria, and it’s been handled by archaeologists and curators and lab technicians for decades, and every one of those people is a modern human whose DNA looks an awful lot like the thing you’re hunting for.
item.content:
The Nobel for medicine went this morning to Svante Pääbo, who worked out how to read the DNA of people who died forty thousand years ago, and I have thought about very little else since about eight.

Here’s the bit that got me, because it isn’t the bit you’d expect.

You’d assume the hard part is that the DNA is old and broken, and it is, it’s in tiny fragments with no instructions attached. But the properly horrible problem is contamination. Bone that old is absolutely full of bacteria, and it’s been handled by archaeologists and curators and lab technicians for decades, and every one of those people is a modern human whose DNA looks an awful lot like the thing you’re hunting for.

So you go looking for a human sequence in an ancient bone and you find one straight away, every time, and the overwhelming likelihood is that it’s yours.

Which means the reading turns out to be a fairly small part of it, and most of the decades went on building a way to prove that what you’ve read is genuinely old. Clean rooms, controls, chemical fingerprints of real age, statistics to catch a fragment that walked in on somebody’s glove. All of that, so that when the answer finally arrives anybody has any reason at all to believe it.

And then the answer arrives, and it’s that one to four percent of the DNA in most people alive outside Africa came from Neanderthals. Which rather changes what the word “extinct” is doing in that sentence.

I love that the prize is really for the not-fooling-yourself. That’s the whole job, in every field I’ve ever been near. Getting a result is easy. Getting a result you’re allowed to trust takes thirty years.

Anyway. Go and read about it. Much nicer than the rest of today’s news.

And it turns out what I liked was having a map I knew, and having routes, and having a spot, and two weeks in I have all of those again about a completely different place, and the fondness transferred over more or less intact while I wasn’t looking.

Which is either a comforting thought or quite a bleak one depending on how much sleep you’ve had, and I’ve had a reasonable amount this week, so today I’m going with comforting.

I find this incredibly comforting for reasons I can’t entirely defend. Something about the fact that the dramatic bit is over and the part that decides whether it counts is a few people patiently measuring the same thing again and again for a month.

Running on about four hours’ sleep and I have a meeting at two. Absolutely worth it.

item.title: Hitting it on purpose

item.title: I couldn't have used them
item.description:

The backups are encrypted. The passphrase is in my password manager. My password manager lives on the machines I was pretending had just burned to the ground.

Two entirely sensible decisions, made about two years apart, which combine into something that doesn’t work. I have known both halves of that for ages and had genuinely never once put them next to each other.

You can’t go back and look at it.

It ran for three months and then it was replaced, and the island I spent all summer in now exists in screenshots and other people’s videos and my own increasingly unreliable memory of roughly where everything was.

Which is presumably obvious to anybody who’s been playing these things for years. It genuinely had not landed on me until tonight.

I don’t think it should be any different, mind. If they’d left the old island up forever it would have turned into a museum instead of a place everybody was in at the same time, and the whole reason it felt like anything was that everybody was in it at once and now nobody is.

Doesn’t make it feel any less strange though.

New season’s up in the small hours. I’ll go and look tomorrow, or the day after.

Funeral in the morning. Everything’s shut.

I’m not going to go. I’ve thought about it properly and it isn’t mine to go and do, and I’d be going for the queue rather than for the thing at the end of the queue, which doesn’t strike me as a good enough reason to take somebody else’s place in it.

I do understand it completely though. Somebody has handed this country a thing that can actually be done, with a beginning and a middle and an end and a clear price in hours, at a point where nothing else on offer to anybody has had any of that about it. Of course there’s a queue. Standing in a line for fourteen hours is something a person can get up and do, whereas the rest of this fortnight has been sitting down and watching other people do things on the telly.

Season ends tomorrow and I’ve got eleven levels left, which has been the other great national emergency round here this week.

Priorities in excellent order, as ever.

Season ends Sunday and I have got about forty levels left to do, which is entirely my own fault and which I will be correcting this week at the expense of both sleep and dignity.

It’s called Vibin’, this one. Started in June, runs to the eighteenth, and the entire theme of it has been summer, chilled out, nice. You plant seeds in the ground and they grow into trees that drop guns, which is gardening, when you think about it, I have spent three months doing horticulture in a shooter. There was ice cream you could eat to make yourself go faster.

The secret skin is Darth Vader, which you unlock by doing Indiana Jones quests, and I would like to be clear that I typed that sentence out and read it back to myself and it does still say what it says.

Then in August they put Dragon Ball in it, so for a few weeks you could Kamehameha somebody off a roof, and there was a cloud you could stand on and fly about. I have no particular attachment to Dragon Ball whatsoever and I did it constantly anyway.

So, six days left, and then the map changes and everything I’ve learned about where to land and which way to run stops being worth anything at all, which I gather happens every three months and which is very obviously the entire point of the thing, although this is the first time I’ve been sorry about it.

The thing I keep thinking though, and I appreciate this is an unreasonable amount of weight to hang on a video game, is that it was called Vibin’ and it has been a genuinely lovely summer in there. Sunny, daft, ice cream, a rave in a mountain, seeds growing into guns. Whereas out here we’ve had forty degrees, a drought, hosepipe bans everywhere except conveniently up here, everybody’s bills going up eighty per cent in one step, and then a fortnight I don’t need to describe to anybody who’s been outside.

None of which got anywhere near it, because why on earth would it.

I don’t think that’s escapism exactly, or if it is then I’ve gone off using escapism as the criticism people use it as. It was somewhere the summer went well. I would have quite liked a summer that went well and I did not get one out here, and I did get about a hundred hours of one in a place where the worst thing that can happen to you is somebody turning up with a better gun.

Forty levels. Six days. Going to be a great deal of Rave Cave.

Back to it.

I’ll find out about October when everybody else does.

item.content:
I have spent today establishing that the spaceship computers I have admired since I was a child would be completely useless to actually own.

Context, if you missed yesterday: I am building a status page for my house, and I have decided it ought to look like a Stargate console, for reasons that would not survive any sort of scrutiny.

So this morning I went and looked at one properly. Not fondly. Professionally, with every intention of stealing from it.

They’re terrible. I’m sorry but they are genuinely terrible.

Everything is enormous. There are about four pieces of actual information on the entire screen. Half the elements are moving and don’t mean anything, because movement reads well on camera and stillness doesn’t. The whole thing is built to be legible to a lens for four seconds while somebody stands in front of it saying something important, and it has never once had to tell you eleven things at the same time, because no scene has ever needed it to.

Whereas a status page has to tell you eleven things at the same time, mostly in order to say that all eleven of them are fine.

So the rule for the rest of the day became: it should feel like the thing, not be the thing. Take the colours. Take the chunky edges. Absolutely take the typeface, that was forty minutes of my one life and I intend to get my money’s worth. But let the layout answer to the hallway rather than the director.

And then, having done all of that very cleverly, I put it on the screen in the hall and walked past it and could not read a single word.

I had built the entire thing sat at a desk with my face about sixty centimetres from a monitor. It lives in a corridor where people see it from three metres away, at an angle, while walking, usually carrying something in both hands.

Everything was too small. The contrast was perfectly fine at a desk and hopeless in a hallway with a window at one end. The most useful sentence on the whole page was sat exactly where your eye arrives last.

There is no clever technique for this. You go and stand where the person stands. That is the entire method, and apparently I need to be taught it again from scratch every single time.

Rebuilt for three metres. It’s uglier and enormously better.

The typeface survived. I’d like that noted.

Right. New Prime Minister tomorrow. Back to the real world in the morning.

The general air of a room in which somebody is about to say “we’re picking up an energy signature”.

I spent forty minutes today choosing a typeface. Forty minutes. For a page that four people will ever look at, in a building where I could simply shout.

In my defence, and I would like a defence, it does solve something real. Nobody here ever tells me when something’s broken, because they don’t want to bother me, because I am perpetually doing something to the server. So the page will say when a thing is broken and also whether I already know about it, which means nobody ever has to stand there weighing up whether it’s worth mentioning.

That’s the justification. It’s a genuinely good justification.

It is not why I’m doing it.

Anyway. New Prime Minister on Monday, apparently. September is being extremely September about everything.

I’m going to go and have an argument with a colour picker.

Apparently the obituaries here and the obituaries there describe two entirely different men, which I gather has been the case for about thirty years.

Posties out tomorrow.

Odd thing, being a bit sad about somebody you only ever knew as a fact.

It’s the last Sunday of August, which I feel rather more than seems reasonable. I get the distinct sense of something being quietly packed away.

Wasps were quiet today, incidentally. Either they’ve moved on or they’re regrouping.

I’ve decided not to look into it.

item.description:
Bank holiday weekend, so three whole days in which to not think about it, and I fully intended to use all of them.

Made it to about half ten.

It isn’t dread, It’s arithmetic. You catch yourself doing sums you never sat down to do, in the queue, filling the kettle, halfway up the stairs, and then you put them away again and they come back later having brought friends.

Bin day’s shifted because of Monday. Posties out again Wednesday.

That’s the shape of the week ahead and, all things considered, I’ll take it.

Posties out today as well, a hundred and fifteen thousand of them, first of four days on strike. Everyone is asking for more money because everything costs more money, and I’m not sure what anybody imagined would happen instead.

It’s still warm out but its not unbearably warm, which makes it a shame that of this landed on a perfectly nice afternoon.

Anyway. Nothing left to count down to.

item.title: Wasps
item.description:
The wasps have started, the proper late August asshole wasps.

I finally looked up why they turn like this, because it happens every single year and I’ve never known. Turns out the colony is basically finished by now. The queen has stopped laying, so there are no grubs left to feed, and it was the grubs that produced the sugary stuff the workers lived on. So the workers have no job and no income and they go off hunting sugar wherever they can find it, which is your pint, and the bin, and the windfall apples fermenting quietly in the grass.

They are, in short, unemployed and drunk and furious about it.

I have never felt closer to them.

Warm today, properly warm. Tomorrow is meant to be the twenty eight. I’ll believe that when it happens, but I have carefully made no plans that would stop me sitting in it.

It’s dark before nine now, which it wasn’t a fortnight ago. That one always gets me. You don’t notice it going and then one evening you look up and the day has simply ended without checking with you first.

The shops have moved on regardless. Pencil cases where the barbecue things were.

Three days.

item.title: GCSEs
item.description:
Monday, and the first properly warm one since he came back. Not twenty eight yet. Building up to it slowly, like he wants us to notice the effort involved.

There’s an education person in the paper today explaining that girls will do better than boys in this week’s GCSEs because the girls revised during lockdown and the boys played PlayStation.

I have read this three times now and it has not improved.

Monday, and the first properly warm one since he came back. Not twenty eight yet. Building up to it slowly, like he wants us to notice the effort involved.

There’s an education person in the paper today explaining that girls will do better than boys in this week’s GCSEs because the girls revised during lockdown and the boys played PlayStation.

I have read this three times now and it has not improved.

I would like to register, from a safe distance of some years, that it is entirely possible to do both. I did both. Simultaneously, on occasion, which I appreciate is not the same as doing either of them well.

The other possibility, which the piece does not trouble itself with, is that a cohort sitting their first real exams after two years of not having any might produce results that resist one tidy explanation. But that won’t go in a headline. PlayStation goes in a headline.

Elsewhere, and considerably less funny, something like 1.7 million households are reckoning on cancelling their energy direct debits. Not switching, not haggling, not ringing up to complain. Cancelling. Which tells you fairly precisely where we’ve got to, four days out. Its a great time to work for an energy company, sigh.

Twenty eight on Wednesday, then. Three days of being pleased about the weather, and then Friday, and then I expect we all go a bit quiet for a while.

item.title: Shapps
item.description:
Trains today, in the loose sense that some of them happened.

Shapps is telling the RMT to put the eight per cent to a vote, and the RMT are telling him where he can put it instead, so I imagine we’ll all be doing this again shortly.

Read something at breakfast that I’ve not been able to put down since. Libraries and museums are working out whether they can operate as warm places this winter, for people who won’t be putting the heating on. Not as a campaign, or a stunt, or a point anybody is making. As a plan. They’re asking for money to do it properly.

So he’s back after all. I withdraw what I said about him yesterday, he was evidently just running late.

It’s a strange pair of things to be holding on the same Sunday, though. Twenty eight on Wednesday, and a library somewhere working out how many chairs it can put out in January.

Fun fact, none of this actually affects me because my job is Work-From-Home and has been since Covid. I don’t miss the commute but I do miss the routine of the office, can’t have one without the other.

Anyway. Cap on Friday.

item.title: Strike day
item.description:
Strike day, so no trains, so I have spent Saturday entirely within walking distance of my own front door.

I want to be clear that I support them completely and also that I had plans.

It’s the signallers that do it. Network Rail are out alongside most of the operators, and once the signallers go it stops mattering who else fancied coming in, the whole thing simply stops working. Thursday they managed about a fifth of the network. Today felt like rather less than that, though I’m going off the app and a general atmosphere rather than anything rigorous.

The one nice part, and I wouldn’t say this to anybody actually striking, is that it’s quiet out there in a way a Saturday never usually is. No day trippers. Everyone who did make it out was on foot and had visibly decided to be cheerful about it, which I found unexpectedly nice to be around.

Ofgem announce the new cap on Friday. Everybody has a number they’re passing about, all of them different, all of them somehow worse than the last one you heard. Nobody actually knows yet, which has not slowed anyone down in the slightest. I’ve decided not to look at any of the predictions, on the grounds that I’ll find out on Friday either way and there is nothing useful to be done with six days of advance dread except sit and have it.

I have of course looked at all of them.

No sign of Helios either, incidentally. I said last time he was due back this week and he has simply not turned up, which after all that fuss I am choosing to take personally.

So it’s been an indoors day, doing the category of job you only ever get to when you can’t leave the house. The sort where you finish, and the room looks precisely the same as it did before, and you’re somehow tired.

Anyway. Trains on Monday, allegedly.

item.title: Heat broke
item.description:
The heat broke on Sunday and I’ve been in a funny mood about it ever since.

I spent most of last week complaining loudly to anybody who would stand still for it that it was too hot to function. Then Helios packed it in, wandered off to bother somebody else, and now it’s nineteen degrees and grey and I find that I miss him. Not enough to want him back but still enough to be annoyed about it.
item.content:
The heat broke on Sunday and I’ve been in a funny mood about it ever since.

I spent most of last week complaining loudly to anybody who would stand still for it that it was too hot to function. Then Helios packed it in, wandered off to bother somebody else, and now it’s nineteen degrees and grey and I find that I miss him. Not enough to want him back but still enough to be annoyed about it.

Monday through Wednesday it hammered it down, which the ground was in no fit state to deal with. That rain that just sits on top of the soil looking at you whereas down south they got proper flooding out of it, sewage on the beaches, warnings, the lot. We got puddles and a smell.

Meanwhile eight parts of England are now officially in drought and we, up here, are not. No hosepipe ban either. I have never in my life been so proud of something I had absolutely no involvement in.

Although.

The Pennine reservoirs are sitting at about half full when they’d usually be three quarters, and Dovestone currently looks like somebody’s pulled the plug out of it. So I think what’s actually happened is that we are in a drought and simply haven’t been informed on the grounds that half the region drinks Lake District rain and the Lake District has never had a dry week in its entire life.

I went up to have a look at our reservoir on Wednesday. In the rain. Like a normal person.

Still working out what this blog is for, incidentally. I had assumed I’d have a theme by now. Instead I have the weather, which is arguably a theme, just not a good one.

Forecast says he’s back next week. Low twenties, nothing dramatic. Which is the correct amount of sun, and therefore nobody will mention it at all.
